hints: A vector needs a direction as well as a magnitude, whereas a scalar needs magnitude only.
For each table entry, ask whether specifying a direction would be needed to state the quantity completely.
walkthrough: Classify each quantity by whether its full specification requires direction as well as magnitude.
Acceleration describes the change of velocity, so it has a direction and is a vector.
Power is the rate of energy transfer and work is energy transferred by a force; neither requires direction, so both are scalars.

ai_rubric.observable: Classifies acceleration as a vector and power and work as scalars; awards 2 marks when all three classifications are correct, or 1 mark when exactly two are correct.

hints: The acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph: find the change in velocity over the time interval.
Read the two endpoints of the plotted section, then calculate (final velocity − initial velocity) / 4.0 s.
walkthrough: For a velocity–time graph, acceleration is the gradient, so use a = Δv / Δt.
The velocity increases from 0.70 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to 1.40 m s⁻¹ at t = 4.0 s.
a = (1.40 − 0.70) / 4.0 = 0.175 m s⁻², which rounds to 0.18 m s⁻².

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the gradient of the velocity–time graph, or an equivalent change-in-velocity-over-time method, with the graph values.
Obtains an acceleration of 0.18 m s⁻², or the unrounded value 0.175 m s⁻².

hints: The displacement from a velocity–time graph is the area between the graph and the time axis.
From 0 to 4.0 s, the straight section forms a trapezium with parallel sides given by the two velocities.
walkthrough: The velocities remain positive, so the distance moved equals the area under the velocity–time graph.
The area is a trapezium with parallel sides 0.70 m s⁻¹ and 1.40 m s⁻¹, separated by 4.0 s.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the area under the velocity–time graph, evaluated as a trapezium or an equivalent rectangle-plus-triangle decomposition.

hints: State force in terms of how an object's momentum changes, rather than as a push or a pull.
The definition must describe a rate: a change in momentum for each unit of time.
walkthrough: Force is defined as the rate of change of momentum.
Equivalently, a resultant force is the change in momentum per unit time.

ai_rubric.observable: Defines force as the rate of change of momentum, or as change of momentum per unit time.

hints: Use F = ma: the resultant force has the same direction as the acceleration, which is the gradient of the velocity–time graph.
Find the three constant-gradient intervals in Fig. 1.1, then transfer their signs and relative magnitudes to three horizontal sections of the force–time graph.
walkthrough: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration, and F = ma means that force has the same sign and relative magnitude as acceleration for a constant mass.
From 0 to 4.0 s, velocity rises linearly, so acceleration and force are constant and positive: draw a horizontal line above the axis.
From 4.0 to 8.0 s, velocity is constant, so acceleration and resultant force are zero: draw a horizontal line on the axis.

From 8.0 to 12.0 s, velocity falls linearly to zero. Its gradient has the opposite sign and twice the magnitude of the first gradient, so draw a horizontal line below the axis at twice the previous distance from it.

ai_rubric.observable: Draws a constant positive force from 0 to 4.0 s.
Draws zero force from 4.0 to 8.0 s.
Draws a constant negative force from 8.0 to 12.0 s with a magnitude greater than the positive force, specifically twice as large from the graph gradients.
